READING 41
EQUITY ISSUANCE AND TRADING
MODULE 41.1: EQUITY MARKETS AND
EXCHANGES
LOS 41.a: Describe primary and secondary public equity markets and their
functions.
Primary equity markets refer to issuance of new securities to the public. Firms
that wish to raise capital by issuing equity securities may use an investment bank
to underwrite the sale of new shares to investors. Typically, the sale will take the
form of an initial public offering (IPO) to investors at large, or a private
placement directly to qualified investors. Primary markets tend to be most
active when share prices are increasing overall.
Some of the circumstances that result in primary equity issuance include the
following:
An early-stage firm wants to expand beyond venture capital financing to attract
new public equity investment.
An existing public company spins off a division as a new public company.
A firm goes public after being restructured by private owners for a number of
years.
A government uses the primary equity market to carry out a full or partial
privatization of an existing state-run entity, transferring its operations to the
private sector.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
We say a company is publicly owned or publicly held when its equity
shares trade in public markets. This is not to be confused with state
ownership of business enterprises. Privatizing a state-run enterprise may
turn it into a publicly owned corporation.

To carry out an IPO, a corporation must fulfill listing and other regulatory
requirements and solicit investors for the new shares. The goals are to introduce
the company to equity analysts and investors, gauge market acceptance,
determine demand, and establish a price range for the prospective issuance.
Figure 41.1 illustrates a typical timeline for an IPO.
Figure 41.1: IPO Timeline
One key IPO requirement is the creation and regulatory review of an equity
prospectus. Elements of an equity prospectus include a description of the
company and its business model; disclosures of key industry and business risks;
audited financial statements; terms of the offering (including the number of
shares to be issued and the expected price range); and use of issuance proceeds.
The prospectus, which is prepared by the issuer and its advisers (including
underwriters), must be approved by the relevant market authorities before the
issuer releases it. Approval does not imply that the regulator endorses the
prospectus or verifies its accuracy.
An equity underwriter assists the firm with raising capital during IPOs or
secondary offerings, such as by determining the pricing of the offer, ensuring
regulatory compliance, or guaranteeing the purchase of the entire offer.
Equity underwriters and the issuer’s owners have an inherent conflict of interest
in an IPO. Although underwriters may generate higher fees with a higher
offering price, in the long run they may benefit more from placing underpriced
shares with institutional investors. Doing so may increase the demand for the
shares included in the offering by institutional investors and encourage investors
to participate in future IPOs. This could be detrimental to the issuer’s owners,
who are most concerned with maximizing the value of the business. This conflict
may contribute to IPOs often being mispriced such that they see significant gains
on the first day of trading.

Less common forms of primary equity issuance include the following:
Direct listing. In a direct listing, a private company goes public by listing its
existing shares on a stock exchange, but without creating any new shares or
raising any new capital.
Special purpose acquisition company (SPAC). A SPAC is a shell company
used to acquire an unspecified private company within a specific time frame
(e.g., two years). A SPAC raises capital through an IPO and immediately places
the net proceeds into a trust account. These funds must either be used within
the specified time period to acquire a private company approved by
shareholders (a de-SPAC transaction), or returned to investors.
Back-door listing. This involves a private firm acquiring a public company to
take advantage of its existing listing.
In contrast to initial offerings, a firm that has previously issued equity securities
may issue additional shares. This is referred to as a seasoned equity offering
and requires a prospectus. These offerings may be dilutive or nondilutive to the
ownership proportions of existing shareholders, depending on whether the shares
being issued are new or already held by existing owners.
A primary follow-on offering involves the sale of new shares. This dilutes
each existing share’s proportional claim to the firm’s net income and assets.
Firms use this method to reduce debt or raise new equity capital.
In a secondary follow-on offering, privately held existing shares (typically
held by founders, insiders, or private equity funds) are sold for the first time in
the public market. This does not change existing shareholders’ proportional
claim to the firm’s net income and assets. A nondilutive offering allows a
firm’s founders and other private investors to decrease their concentrated
ownership position and diversify their holdings.
After shares have been issued, subsequent trades occur in the secondary equity
markets. Secondary markets provide existing shareholders with liquidity and
allow new investors to purchase an interest in a company. Secondary markets are
active regardless of the direction of the market.
Observed market prices in the secondary market allow investors, analysts, and
other stakeholders to assess periodic share returns, volatilities, and correlations
across periods of time, and to gauge a company’s performance. For issuers, share
price information provides feedback to support decision-making, financing, and
compensation. Firms wishing to raise additional equity capital or distribute

capital to shareholders will generally factor secondary market pricing and
trading into their decision-making process. Firms that use restricted stock units
(RSUs) and other share-based compensation use secondary market price changes
to evaluate performance.
LOS 41.b: Compare exchange, off-exchange, and over-the-counter equities
trading.
An equity exchange is a rules-based venue where market participants trade
equity securities on a regular basis. Trading rules establish regularly scheduled
trading hours and promote liquidity and transparency. An exchange-traded
equity market structure consists of broker-dealers, financial intermediaries that
work with investors to execute trades. Each broker-dealer routes orders through
a centralized exchange order matching system that is used to pair buy and sell
orders for shares.
Broker-dealers act either on behalf of clients as an agent, or as a principal
counterparty to a financial transaction with a client. Most often, stock exchanges
designate a single dealer, known as designated market maker, to ensure
continuous trading of each listed security. The designated market maker is
responsible for purchasing, holding, or selling shares to promote liquidity and
price discovery during normal market hours and times of market imbalance or
high volatility.
Securities dealers provide prices at which they will buy and sell shares. The bid
price is the price at which a dealer will buy a security. The ask price or offer
price is the price at which a dealer will sell a security.
The difference between the bid and ask prices is referred to as the bid-ask
spread or bid-offer spread and is the source of a dealer’s compensation. This
spread represents the cost of purchasing and selling shares in the current market.
The bid-ask spread at any given time is the difference between the lowest ask
price and the highest bid price.
A bid-ask spread may be expressed as a percentage of the lowest ask price:
PROFESSOR’S NOTE

From an investor’s perspective, remember that you always get the side
of a bid-ask spread that is worse for you. If you are buying a security,
you must pay the higher price (the ask). If you are selling, you only get
the lower price (the bid).
This “worse for you” rule is especially useful with foreign exchange
transactions. As you will see in the Level II curriculum, whether the bid
or ask price applies depends on which way around an exchange rate is
quoted. Nevertheless, the bid or ask price you get is always the one that
gives you less of the currency you are acquiring.
The most common orders, in terms of execution instructions, are market or limit
orders. A market order instructs the broker to execute the trade immediately at
the best available price. A limit order places a minimum execution price on sell
orders or a maximum execution price on buy orders. For example, a buy order
with a limit of $6 will be executed immediately if the market ask price is $6 or
less, but if the market price is greater than $6, the order will remain unexecuted
unless the market price decreases to $6 or less.
Market depth is the relative size of orders posted at or near the best available
bid and offer prices or the mid-market price, the average of the lowest ask and
highest bid:
Figure 41.2 shows market depth as a function of market price, with limit buy
orders at low prices and limit sell orders at high prices.
Figure 41.2: Equity Limit Order Book1

Market participants may track intraday share performance using a volume-
weighted average price (VWAP). This measure is derived by weighting the
trade price by the volume of shares traded over a specified period:
Off-exchange trading usually involves either illiquid equities with low trading
volumes, or large orders known as block trades. Block trades are usually
defined as orders of 10,000 shares or more.
Off-exchange trading looks to minimize the implicit costs of trading. These are
the indirect and unobservable costs resulting from the market impact of trading
and arise from the following sources:
Market impact. This is the effect on transaction prices of executing a large
trade immediately.
Delay costs (slippage). This is the inability to complete a desired trade
immediately.
Opportunity costs. This is unrealized profit that results from a failure to
execute a trade quickly.

Over-the-counter (OTC) trading, or quote-driven trading, involves a network
of broker-dealers who act as market makers, displaying bid and ask prices. The
prices they display are firm quotes, meaning they must execute orders received
at those prices. Each broker-dealer works with others to route trades by
executing offsetting buy or sell orders. OTC markets offer less transparency than
exchange-traded markets. Traders may or may not be executing trades at the best
available price.
Dealers usually maintain an inventory of securities. Quote-driven markets are
sometimes called dealer markets, price-driven markets, or OTC markets. Most
securities other than stocks trade in quote-driven markets, and trading often takes
place electronically.

MODULE 41.2: EQUITY INDEXES AND LIQUIDITY
MEASURES
LOS 41.c: Describe liquidity measures for a publicly listed security and
calculate float and average daily volume.
A firm’s market float is the total value of the shares that are available to the
investing public. This excludes the value of shares held by controlling
stockholders because they are unlikely to sell their shares.
market float = total shares outstanding − restricted shares or shares not available for trading

A stock’s average daily volume represents its average number of shares traded
in a day, measured over a given period:
The turnover ratio is the ratio of average daily volume to market float and
indicates the proportion of outstanding shares that are exchanged on a given
trading day:
These metrics allow investors to gauge their ability to liquidate positions based
on market activity, as the following example illustrates.
EXAMPLE: Liquidating an equity position
Southern Pension Plan owns 600,000 shares of Neptune Corporation. The
average daily volume in Neptune over the last month has been 2,250,000
shares. Southern’s internal trading guidelines prohibit the fund from buying or
selling more than 6% of a stock’s average daily trading volume on any given
day. Southern’s chief investment officer has instructed the plan’s trading staff
to fully liquidate the plan’s holdings in Neptune shares. Calculate the number
of days necessary to complete the liquidation.

four days, but it may complete the sale within five days.
Market depth and breadth indicate the ability of a market to execute trades
without having a significant unfavorable impact on price. Secondary equity
market liquidity measures include the following:
Market depth. This is the relative size of orders posted at or near the best
available bid and offer prices.
Market breadth. This measures the number of orders at different price levels
both above and below, but close to, the best bid and offer prices.

Market resiliency. This is the ability of an issuer’s shares to maintain a stable
market-clearing price at which all buy and sell orders can be executed. In a
more resilient market, the stock price will adjust more quickly to a new
market-clearing price following a shock.
LOS 41.d: Describe types of equity indexes.
A security market index is used to represent the performance of an asset class,
security market, or segment of a market. They are usually created as portfolios
of individual securities, which are referred to as the constituent securities of the
index. An index has a numerical value that is calculated from the market prices
(actual when available or estimated) of its constituent securities at a point in
time.
Investors can use various equity market indexes when evaluating performance
and benchmarking investment and investment managers. These equity indexes
can be classified as follows:
Broad-based equity indexes include the largest listed firms adjusted by market
float and calculated on a market-capitalization-weighted basis. They may be
tiered based on issuer size. A composite market index measures a market’s
overall performance and usually contains more than 90% of a market’s total
value. For example, the Wilshire 5000 Index contains more than 6,000 equity
securities and is, therefore, a good representation of the overall performance of
the US equity market.
Sector indexes measure the returns for an industry sector, such as health care,
financial, or consumer goods firms. Investors can use these indexes in cyclical
analysis because some sectors perform better than others in various phases of
the business cycle. Sector indexes can be for a particular country or global.
These indexes are used to evaluate portfolio managers and construct index
portfolios.
Investment theme indexes can be created based on investor trends beyond
selecting a certain industry or company size. For example, an index may
contain issuers that have been screened to comply with environmental, social,
and governance (ESG) principles (e.g., S&P Europe ESG 350 Index).
An example of indexes with alternative weighting methods is an equally
weighted index based on the same companies included in a broad-based index.
The goal is to reduce the biases of the greater weighting given to the largest

companies. Factor-based investing, which is investment selection based on
fundamental factors that may drive performance, has also been a driver of
indexes based on alternative weighting (e.g., MSCI Quality Indexes).
Multi-market indexes are typically constructed from the indexes of markets in
several countries and used to measure the equity returns of a geographic region
(e.g., Latin America indexes), markets based on their stage of economic
development (e.g., emerging markets indexes), or the entire world (e.g., MSCI
World Index).
MODULE QUIZ 41.2
1. Market float of a stock is best described as its:
A. total outstanding shares.
B. shares that are available to domestic investors.
C. outstanding shares, excluding those held by controlling shareholders.
2. The relative size of orders posted at or near the best available bid and offer prices is best
described as a market’s:
A. depth.
B. breadth.
C. resiliency.
3. A public company has 10.5 million shares outstanding and 2.0 million restricted shares.
The firm’s market float is:
A. 8.5 million shares.
B. 10.5 million shares.
C. 12.5 million shares.
4. A security market index is best described as a:
A. value used to adjust nominal security prices for the effects of inflation.
B. directory of ticker symbols for the securities listed on a given market.
C. group of securities selected to represent the performance of a security market.
KEY CONCEPTS
LOS 41.a
Primary equity markets refer to the issuance of new securities to the public. The
IPO process involves fulfilling requirements such as an equity prospectus, and
soliciting investors for the new publicly listed shares.
Secondary equity markets are where trades occur after their initial issuance.
Observed market prices in the secondary market allow investors to assess returns
and gauge company performance.

LOS 41.b
An equity exchange is a rules-based venue where market participants trade
equity securities on a regular basis.
Off-exchange trading usually involves block trades (usually defined as an order
of 10,000 shares of more) or equities that are illiquid or exhibit low trading
volumes.
Over-the-counter (OTC) equity trading involves a network of broker-dealers
who buy and sell shares among themselves. OTC markets offer less transparency
than exchange-traded markets.
LOS 41.c
A firm’s market float is the total value of the shares available to the investing
public, excluding shares held by controlling stockholders.
Average daily volume is the average number of issuer shares traded each day
over a given period.
The turnover ratio is the ratio of average daily volume to market float and
indicates the proportion of outstanding shares exchanged on a given trading day.
Other equity market liquidity measures include market depth, market breadth,
and market resiliency.
LOS 41.d
A security market index is used to represent the performance of an asset class,
security market, or segment of a market. Equity indexes can be classified as
broad based, sector, investment theme, alternatively weighted, and multi-market.
ANSWER KEY FOR MODULE QUIZZES
Module Quiz 41.1

41.a)
. C Trading rules are used to promote liquidity, provide transparency, and
establish regularly scheduled trading hours. (LOS 41.b)
. A A dealer will buy a security at the bid price or will sell a security at the ask
price. (LOS 41.b)

Module Quiz 41.2
. C Market float represents shares available to the investing public and
excludes shares held by controlling shareholders. (LOS 41.c)
. A Market depth is the relative size of orders posted at or near the best
available bid and offer prices. (LOS 41.c)

million shares outstanding and 2.0 million restricted shares, the firm’s
market float is 8.5 million shares. (LOS 41.c)
. C A security market index is a group of securities (constituent securities)
designed to represent the performance of an asset class, security market, or
market segment. (LOS 41.d)
